summary: This memo describes a proposed Simple File Transfer Protocol, aimed at being more useful than TFTP but easier to implement than FTP. It supports access control, transfers, directory listing and changing, renaming, and deleting. It is historic and not the later SSH file transfer protocol.

eli5.summary: A middle-sized way to send files: easier to build than the full version, yet able to do more than the tiniest one.

questions: what is the simple file transfer protocol
sftp versus tftp and ftp in 1984
subtitle: A middle-ground file transfer protocol between TFTP and FTP

tldr.problem: TFTP was too simple (no user access control, limited commands) and FTP was too complex to implement, leaving no option for systems that wanted basic file transfer with authentication and directory operations.
tldr.mechanism: SFTP uses a single TCP connection where clients send four-letter ASCII commands (USER, PASS, RETR, STOR, etc.) and receive response codes and messages. It supports login with user id and password, file transfers in ASCII or binary mode, directory listing and changing, file renaming and deletion.
tldr.outcome: SFTP provided a simpler alternative to FTP for basic file transfer needs, though it is now historic and has been superseded by more modern protocols. The name was reused decades later for the SSH File Transfer Protocol, which is completely different.

today: RFC 913 is a historic document published in September 1984. SFTP as defined in this RFC is no longer in use and has been superseded by more modern file transfer protocols. The acronym SFTP was later reused for the SSH File Transfer Protocol (part of the SSH suite), which is a completely different protocol designed for secure remote access.

sections.title: The SFTP Protocol
sections.content:
Simple File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) fills the gap between TFTP and FTP. TFTP is extremely minimal—no user authentication, no directory operations, and only the simplest command set. FTP is powerful but complex to implement. SFTP adds user access control and richer operations compared to TFTP, while staying simpler than FTP.

SFTP can be implemented over any reliable 8-bit byte stream protocol; RFC 913 specifies the TCP version. Unlike FTP, which uses two TCP connections (one for control, one for data transfer via a separate data connection) and TFTP (which uses UDP), SFTP uses only a single TCP connection. Clients connect to port 115 and send commands and receive replies over the same connection.
sections.eli5: SFTP is a way to send files that is not as basic as TFTP but not as fancy as FTP.

sections.title: Commands and Responses
sections.content:
SFTP commands are sent as four ASCII letters (case insensitive) followed by a space, arguments, and a null terminator. The simplest form uses just four letters and null when no arguments are needed. The server replies with a response code character (immediately, with no space) followed by an optional ASCII message string and a null terminator.

Response codes include: plus sign for success, minus sign for error, exclamation mark for state changes like successful login, and hash mark followed by decimal digits for numeric responses. An error response starts with the minus sign followed by an explanation message. Commands accepted are USER, ACCT, PASS, TYPE, LIST, CDIR, KILL, NAME, TOBE, DONE, RETR, STOR and SEND.
sections.eli5: Commands are four letters like USER or STOR, and the server answers with a success sign for yes or a minus sign for no, plus a short message.

sections.title: Session Flow and Authentication
sections.content:
A session starts when the client connects to port 115. The server sends a greeting (either +hostname SFTP Service for success or –hostname message if it is not accepting connections). If the server sends the error code, it closes the connection. Otherwise, the client sends USER userid. The server may reply with ! (user is already logged in), + (user valid, send account/password), or the error code (invalid user, try again).

The client then sends ACCT account and/or PASS password as needed, receiving replies that may require the other one or confirm login with !. Only after receiving a ! response from the login sequence can the client send other commands: TYPE to set transfer mode, LIST to list directories, CDIR to change directory, KILL to delete files, NAME/TOBE to rename, RETR to retrieve files, STOR to store files, and DONE to finish. This flow ensures user authentication before allowing file operations.
sections.eli5: First you connect and say who you are, then you prove your password, and only then can you ask for files or list directories.

sections.title: File Transfer Modes and Operations
sections.content:
The TYPE command sets how file data is encoded. TYPE A (ASCII) converts the local end-of-line convention to CRLF on transmission using NETASCII rules, the same as Telnet. TYPE B (Binary) sends 8-bit bytes as is. TYPE C (Continuous) sends bits continuously without regard to word boundaries, useful for systems like TOPS-20 where the word size is not a multiple of 8 bits. Example: a TOPS-20 page of 512 36-bit words contains 18432 bits or 2304 8-bit bytes in continuous mode.

For RETR file (retrieve), the server replies with the byte count if successful (as ASCII digits) or an error response if the file doesn't exist. The client then sends SEND to receive the file stream or STOP if it cannot accept the data. For STOR (store), the client specifies NEW (create a new generation), OLD (overwrite), or APP (append). The server confirms, the client sends SIZE bytes, then the file data. For LIST, F specifies formatted (file names only) and V specifies verbose (names plus sizes, dates, and other metadata).
sections.eli5: You can send files in text or binary mode, and you can list directories, rename files, or delete files, all using simple commands and replies.

sections.title: Example Session
sections.content:
An example session shows the message sequence. When a client connects, the server sends +MIT-XX SFTP Service. The client sends USER MKL. The server replies +MKL ok, send password. The client sends PASS foo. The server replies ! MKL logged in. Now the client can operate. It sends LIST F PS:<MKL> and receives a formatted directory listing. Then LIST V for verbose. Then RETR SMALL.FILE and the server replies with the byte count (69). The client sends SEND, receives the file data (69 bytes, no null terminator), and sends DONE to close the connection.

The design aims for clarity in debugging: commands are ASCII text, not binary codes. The RFC editor notes in the appendix that while binary operation codes would be more efficient, ASCII commands were chosen because the extra programming cost is minimal and the transmission cost is trivial, while the benefit of easier debugging is significant.
sections.eli5: The client and server talk back and forth in plain words, not binary numbers, so if something goes wrong it is easy to see what happened.
